dryRun.title: Where is x looked up? (scope chain)
rows: a function defined in global but called inside outer
dryRun.note: Scope is lexical: a function looks up names where it was written, not where it is called. Each { } block (with let/const) and each function makes a new scope.

think.q:
const x = 'global'
function show() { return x }
function run() { const x = 'local'; return show() }
console.log(run())
why: show was written at the top level, so it sees the global x. Where it is called does not matter.

think.q:
let n = 1
{ let n = 2; { n = 3 } }
console.log(n)
why: The inner n = 3 assigns to the nearest n, the block one. The outer n is untouched.

think.q:
function f() { y = 5 }
f()
console.log(typeof y)
why: Assigning to an undeclared name in sloppy mode creates a global variable. In strict mode (and in modules) it throws instead.

think.q:
const items = [1, 2]
for (const i of items) { const sq = i * i }
console.log(typeof sq, typeof i)
why: Both sq and i live only inside the loop body block.

think.q: Why is lexical scope what makes closures possible?
opts: A function keeps access to the variables of the place it was written, even after that place has finished running
Because functions copy all variables when called
why: The next lessons rely on this: the scope chain is fixed at write time.

try.task: Write makeIdGenerator(prefix) that returns a function giving prefix-1, prefix-2… Each generator has its own count, and nothing leaks into the global scope.
try.hint: Keep the counter in a let inside makeIdGenerator.

checks.verify: const a = makeIdGenerator("u"); assert(a() === "u-1" && a() === "u-2", "sequence")

checks.t: each generator has its own counter
checks.verify: const a = makeIdGenerator("a"), b = makeIdGenerator("b"); a(); a(); assert(b() === "b-1", "separate")
const before = Object.keys(globalThis).length; makeIdGenerator("z")(); assert(Object.keys(globalThis).length === before, "leaked a global")

takeaway.key: Scope is decided where code is written. Lookups walk outwards: block → function → … → global.
mistakes: Assigning to an undeclared name and creating a global by accident.
Thinking a function sees the variables of its caller.

dryRun.title: What exists before the first line runs
dryRun.note: Before running a scope, JavaScript registers every declaration in it. Function declarations are ready to call; var starts as undefined; let, const and class exist but are in the temporal dead zone until their line runs.

think.q:
console.log(typeof hi, typeof bye)
function hi() {}
var bye = function () {}
why: The function declaration is hoisted whole. bye is a var: its name exists but its value is still undefined.

think.q:
try { console.log(x) } catch (e) { console.log(e.constructor.name) }
let x = 1
why: x is in the temporal dead zone until its let line runs, so reading it throws a ReferenceError.
think.exec:
try { console.log(x) } catch (e) { console.log(e.constructor.name) }
let x = 1

think.q:
var v = 'outer'
function f() { console.log(v); var v = 'inner' }
f()
why: Inside f, the local var v is hoisted to the top of f, shadowing the outer one, and is undefined at the log.

think.q:
let t = 'outer'
function g() { try { return t } finally {} ; let t = 'inner' }
try { g() } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) }
why: The local let t exists for the whole function body but is in the TDZ before its line. It shadows the outer t, so reading it throws.

think.q: Why did let/const get a temporal dead zone instead of starting as undefined like var?
opts: So reading a variable before it is set is a loud error instead of a silent undefined
Because const has no value yet
why: A silent undefined hides bugs. The TDZ turns them into a clear ReferenceError.

try.task: Write whatHappens(code): run a snippet with new Function(code) and return "ok", or the error name (e.g. "ReferenceError") if it throws. Then use it to confirm the TDZ cases.
try.hint: Wrap the call in try/catch and return e.name.

checks.verify: assert(whatHappens("let a = 1; return a") === "ok", "ok")

checks.t: reading let/const before the line is a ReferenceError
checks.verify: assert(whatHappens("return b; let b = 1") === "ReferenceError" && whatHappens("c; const c = 1") === "ReferenceError", "TDZ")

checks.t: var and function declarations do not throw
checks.verify: assert(whatHappens("v; var v = 1") === "ok" && whatHappens("f(); function f() {}") === "ok", "hoisted")

takeaway.key: Function declarations are fully hoisted, var starts as undefined, let/const/class are in the TDZ until their line.
mistakes: Calling a function expression or arrow before its line.
A local declaration later in a function shadowing an outer name for the whole function.

dryRun.title: Call stack for: main() → a() → b()
dryRun.note: Every call creates an execution context (its variables, its this, a link to the outer scope) and pushes it on the call stack. Returning pops it. JavaScript runs one context at a time.

think.q:
function a() { console.log('a start'); b(); console.log('a end') }
function b() { console.log('b') }
a()
why: b runs completely, in the middle of a, then control returns to a.

think.q:
function depth(n) { try { return depth(n + 1) } catch { return n > 1000 } }
console.log(depth(0))
why: Infinite recursion keeps pushing contexts until the stack overflows (RangeError). It is caught at the deepest level, where n is far above 1000.
think.exec:
function depth(n) { try { return depth(n + 1) } catch { return n > 1000 } }
console.log(depth(0))

think.q:
function outer() { const x = 1; return function inner() { return x } }
const fn = outer()
console.log(fn())
why: outer's context was popped, but inner still holds a link to outer's variables. That link is a closure (next lesson).

think.q:
console.log(1)
setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0)
console.log(3)
why: The timeout callback can only run when the stack is empty, after the whole script finishes. (The event loop lesson covers this.)
think.exec:
console.log(1)
setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0)
console.log(3)

think.q: A stack trace shows the same function 10,000 times and "Maximum call stack size exceeded". Most likely cause?
opts: A memory leak in a Map
Recursion with a missing or wrong base case
why: A while loop freezes the page but does not grow the stack. Only unbounded nested calls overflow it.

try.task: Write sumTo(n) that adds 1..n without recursion, so sumTo(1e6) does not blow the stack, and sumToRec(n) recursively. Compare them on a large n.
try.hint: A loop uses one context. The recursive version adds one context per call.

checks.verify: assert(sumTo(4) === 10 && sumToRec(4) === 10, "small")

checks.t: the loop version handles a million
the recursive version overflows on a million
checks.verify: let threw = false; try { sumToRec(1e6) } catch (e) { threw = e instanceof RangeError }; assert(threw, "expected a RangeError")

takeaway.key: Each call pushes an execution context on the call stack; return pops it. One thing runs at a time.
mistakes: Unbounded recursion: "Maximum call stack size exceeded".
Thinking a setTimeout(…, 0) callback runs before the current code finishes.

dryRun.title: const c = makeCounter(); c(); c()
dryRun.note: A closure is a function plus the variables of the scope it was created in. They stay alive as long as the function does. Every call of the outer function creates a fresh set.

think.q:
function makeCounter() { let c = 0; return () => ++c }
const a = makeCounter(), b = makeCounter()
a(); a()
console.log(a(), b())
why: a and b each have their own c.

think.q:
const fns = []
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) fns.push(() => i)
console.log(fns.map((f) => f()).join(''))
why: All three closures share the same var i, which is 3 after the loop.

think.q:
function once(fn) { let done = false, r; return (...a) => done ? r : (done = true, r = fn(...a)) }
const init = once((x) => x * 2)
console.log(init(5), init(100))
why: The closure remembers done and the first result, so later calls return 10 again.

think.q:
let x = 1
const f = () => x
x = 2
console.log(f())
why: A closure keeps a live link to the variable, not a copy of its value at creation time.
think.exec:
let x = 1
const f = () => x
x = 2
console.log(f())

think.q: A closure holds a reference to a 50 MB array it never uses again. What happens?
opts: It is freed when the outer function returns
JavaScript copies only what is used, always
The array cannot be garbage collected while the closure is reachable
why: Keep long-lived closures (event handlers, timers, caches) from capturing big data they do not need.

try.task: Write createBank(initial) returning { deposit(n), withdraw(n), balance() }. The balance must be private (no property to change it), and withdraw must throw if there is not enough money.
try.hint: Keep let balance inside createBank; the three methods close over it.

checks.t: deposit and withdraw change the balance
checks.verify: const a = createBank(100); a.deposit(50); a.withdraw(30); assert(a.balance() === 120, "balance")
const a = createBank(10); let t = false; try { a.withdraw(11) } catch { t = true }; assert(t && a.balance() === 10, "must throw and keep balance")
const a = createBank(5); a.balance = () => 1e9; const b = createBank(5); assert(b.balance() === 5 && Object.keys(createBank(1)).every((k) => typeof createBank(1)[k] === "function"), "no data fields")

takeaway.key: A closure is a function that remembers its birth scope. Use it for private state; remember it also keeps that state alive.
mistakes: var in loops with callbacks.
Accidentally capturing large objects in long-lived handlers.
Expecting a closure to hold a snapshot value instead of a live variable.

dryRun.title: (function () { const secret = 1 })()
rows: turns the function into an expression
dryRun.note: An IIFE creates a private scope and runs once. Before ES modules and let/const, it was the standard way to avoid globals; today you still meet it in older code and for one-off setup.

think.q:
const counter = (() => { let n = 0; return { inc: () => ++n } })()
counter.inc(); counter.inc()
console.log(counter.inc(), typeof n)
why: The IIFE ran once and returned an object whose method closes over n. n itself is not visible outside.

think.q:
var result = (function (a, b) { return a + b })(2, 3)
console.log(result)
why: The IIFE is called with 2 and 3 immediately, so result holds 5, not a function.
think.exec:
var result = (function (a, b) { return a + b })(2, 3)
console.log(result)

think.q:
const x = 'outer';
(function () { const x = 'inner' })()
console.log(x)
why: The inner x lives only in the IIFE's own scope.

think.q:
const r = (async () => 42)()
console.log(r instanceof Promise)
why: An async IIFE returns a Promise. It is a common way to use await in a script without top-level await.
think.exec:
const r = (async () => 42)()
console.log(r instanceof Promise)

think.q: Why are the wrapping parentheses needed in (function () {})()?
opts: Without them, a line starting with function is a declaration, which cannot be called in place
why: The parentheses make the parser read it as an expression.

try.task: Write makeConfig as an IIFE (the variable holds the result, not a function) that exposes get(key) and set(key, value) over a private object. set must reject unknown keys; the known keys are theme ("light") and lang ("en").
try.hint: const makeConfig = (() => { const data = {...}; return { get, set } })()
try.starter: const makeConfig = undefined // replace with an IIFE

checks.verify: assert(makeConfig.get("theme") === "light" && makeConfig.get("lang") === "en", "defaults")
makeConfig.set("lang", "hi"); assert(makeConfig.get("lang") === "hi", "set")

checks.t: unknown keys are rejected and data is private
checks.verify: let t = false; try { makeConfig.set("color", 1) } catch { t = true }; assert(t && !("data" in makeConfig), "private")

takeaway.key: An IIFE runs once and gives you a private scope. Modules replaced most uses, but the pattern (and async IIFEs) still appear.
mistakes: Forgetting the semicolon before a line that starts with (.
Assigning the function instead of calling it.

dryRun.title: Arrow vs normal function
dryRun.note: Arrows are short, but the big difference is this: an arrow has no this of its own and uses the one from where it was written. That makes them great as callbacks inside methods, and wrong as methods themselves.

think.q:
const o = { n: 1, normal() { return this.n }, arrow: () => typeof this }
console.log(o.normal(), o.arrow())
why: The method gets this = o, so 1.
The arrow has no this of its own: it uses the top-level this (the global object in a plain script), so typeof this is "object", and it is not o.
think.exec:
const o = { n: 1, normal() { return this.n }, arrow: () => typeof this }
console.log(o.normal(), o.arrow())

think.q:
const timer = { s: 0, start() { [1, 2, 3].forEach(() => this.s++); return this.s } }
console.log(timer.start())
why: The arrow callback uses start's this, which is timer. A normal function callback would get undefined/global this.
think.exec:
const timer = { s: 0, start() { [1, 2, 3].forEach(() => this.s++); return this.s } }
console.log(timer.start())

think.q:
const f = () => ({ a: 1 })
const g = () => { a: 1 }
console.log(f().a, g())
why: { a: 1 } after an arrow is read as a block with a label a:, so g returns undefined. Wrap an object literal in parentheses.

think.q:
const A = () => {}
try { new A() } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) }
why: Arrows cannot be constructors.
think.exec:
const A = () => {}
try { new A() } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) }

think.q: Which is a bad place for an arrow function?
opts: A setTimeout callback inside a method
A small helper like const add = (a, b) => a + b
An object method that uses this
why: As a method, the arrow would not get the object as this.

try.task: Write makeTimer() returning { ticks: 0, tick(n) } where tick(n) uses Array.from({ length: n }).forEach(...) to add 1 to this.ticks n times and returns the new total. Use the right kind of function in each place.
try.hint: Method: shorthand (gets this). Callback inside: arrow (reuses that this).

checks.verify: const t = makeTimer(); assert(t.tick(3) === 3, "3")
const t = makeTimer(); t.tick(3); assert(t.tick(2) === 5 && t.ticks === 5, "5")
const a = makeTimer(), b = makeTimer(); a.tick(4); assert(b.tick(1) === 1, "independent")

takeaway.key: Arrows have no own this, arguments or prototype. Use them for callbacks; use normal method syntax for methods.
mistakes: Arrow functions as object methods.
Returning an object literal without parentheses.

dryRun.title: What decides this (most important first)
dryRun.note: this is decided by how a function is called, not where it is written (arrows are the exception). Losing the dot loses the object.

think.q:
'use strict'
const user = { name: 'A', hi() { return this?.name } }
const hi = user.hi
console.log(user.hi(), hi())
why: Called as user.hi(), this is user. Copied out and called plainly, this is undefined in strict mode, so this?.name is undefined.
think.exec:
'use strict'
const user = { name: 'A', hi() { return this?.name } }
const hi = user.hi
console.log(user.hi(), hi())

think.q:
const o = { v: 1, get() { return this.v } }
const p = { v: 2, get: o.get }
console.log(p.get())
why: The function is shared, but it is called as p.get(), so this is p.

think.q:
function Person(n) { this.n = n }
const x = new Person('z')
console.log(x.n)
why: With new, this is a fresh object which is returned automatically.

think.q:
'use strict'
const btn = { label: 'ok', click() { setTimeout(function () { console.log(this === btn) }, 0) } }
btn.click()
why: A plain callback passed to setTimeout is not called as btn.something(), so it does not get btn as this. (In Node it is a Timeout object, in browsers the window.) Use an arrow.

think.q: button.addEventListener("click", this.save) inside a class throws "Cannot read properties of undefined". Best fix?
why: Passing this.save detaches it from the object. Wrap it in an arrow, or bind it once in the constructor.

try.task: Write bindAll(obj): replace every function-valued own property of obj with a version bound to obj, so methods can be passed around as callbacks. Return obj.
examples: const c = bindAll({ n: 1, get() { return this.n } }); const g = c.get; g()  // 1
try.hint: Loop over Object.keys(obj); for functions do obj[k] = obj[k].bind(obj).

checks.t: a detached method still sees the object
checks.verify: const c = bindAll({ n: 1, get() { return this.n } }); const g = c.get; assert(g() === 1, "this lost")
const o = bindAll({ x: 1, s: "a" }); assert(o.x === 1 && o.s === "a", "values")
const c = bindAll({ total: 0, add(v) { this.total += v } }); [1, 2, 3].forEach(c.add); assert(c.total === 6, "callback")

takeaway.key: this = how the function is called: new → new object, call/apply/bind → given value, obj.fn() → obj, plain call → undefined (strict). Arrows inherit it.
mistakes: Passing obj.method as a callback and losing this.
Expecting this inside a nested normal function to be the outer object.

dryRun.title: fn = function (a, b) { return this.x + a + b }, obj = { x: 1 }
dryRun.note: call and apply invoke now with a chosen this (apply takes an array). bind returns a new function with this (and optionally some arguments) locked in. A bound function cannot be re-bound.

think.q:
function greet(g, p) { return g + ' ' + this.name + p }
console.log(greet.call({ name: 'A' }, 'hi', '!'), greet.apply({ name: 'B' }, ['yo', '?']))
why: call takes the arguments one by one, apply as an array. Same result shape.
think.exec:
function greet(g, p) { return g + ' ' + this.name + p }
console.log(greet.call({ name: 'A' }, 'hi', '!'), greet.apply({ name: 'B' }, ['yo', '?']))

think.q:
function f() { return this.v }
const b = f.bind({ v: 1 })
console.log(b.call({ v: 2 }), b.bind({ v: 3 })())
why: Once bound, this is fixed. call and a second bind cannot change it.

think.q: console.log(Math.max.apply(null, [3, 9, 2]), Math.max(...[3, 9, 2]))
why: apply spreads an array into arguments, which is what spread syntax does today.
think.exec: console.log(Math.max.apply(null, [3, 9, 2]), Math.max(...[3, 9, 2]))

think.q:
const add = (a, b) => a + b
const add5 = add.bind(null, 5)
console.log(add5(10), add5.length)
why: bind can pre-fill arguments (partial application). The bound function's length drops by the number of pre-filled args.

think.q: What does arrowFn.call(obj) do to this inside an arrow function?
opts: Nothing: arrows ignore call/apply/bind for this
why: Arrows always use the outer this. Arguments still pass through.

try.task: Implement myBind(fn, ctx, ...preset) without using bind: return a function that calls fn with this = ctx and the preset arguments followed by new ones.
examples: myBind(function (a, b) { return this.x + a + b }, { x: 1 }, 2)(3)  // 6

checks.verify: assert(myBind(function () { return this.x }, { x: 7 })() === 7, "this")

checks.t: preset and later arguments combine in order
checks.verify: assert(myBind(function (a, b, c) { return [a, b, c].join("") }, null, "a", "b")("c") === "abc", "args")

checks.t: the original function is not changed
checks.verify: function f() { return this && this.x }; const b = myBind(f, { x: 1 }); assert(typeof b === "function" && b() === 1 && f.call({ x: 2 }) === 2, "original changed or not bound")

takeaway.key: call/apply: run now with a chosen this. bind: make a new function with this (and args) fixed for good.
mistakes: Using bind and expecting a later call() to override it.
Using call/apply on arrow functions to change this.

dryRun.title: [1, 2, 3, 4].filter(isEven).map(double).reduce(sum, 0)
dryRun.note: A higher-order function takes a function or returns one. map, filter and reduce take callbacks and return new arrays (or a value) without changing the original.

think.q: console.log([1, 2, 3].map((x, i) => x * i))
why: map passes (value, index, array). 1×0, 2×1, 3×2.
think.exec: console.log([1, 2, 3].map((x, i) => x * i))

think.q: console.log(['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt))
why: map passes the index as parseInt's radix: parseInt("1", 0) = 1, parseInt("2", 1) = NaN, parseInt("3", 2) = NaN. Use map(Number) or an arrow.
think.exec: console.log(['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt))

think.q:
console.log([].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0))
try { [].reduce((a, b) => a + b) } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) }
why: With an initial value an empty array returns it. Without one, reduce on an empty array throws a TypeError.
think.exec:
console.log([].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0))
try { [].reduce((a, b) => a + b) } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) }

think.q:
const arr = [3, 1, 2]
const sorted = arr.toSorted()
arr.sort()
console.log(sorted === arr, arr.join(''))
why: toSorted returns a new array. sort sorts in place and returns the same array.
think.exec:
const arr = [3, 1, 2]
const sorted = arr.toSorted()
arr.sort()
console.log(sorted === arr, arr.join(''))

think.q: You need the first user with age over 30, or undefined. Which?
why: find returns the element (stops early). filter returns an array, some returns a boolean.

try.task: Write myMap(arr, fn), myFilter(arr, fn) and myReduce(arr, fn, init) without using the built-ins. Callbacks receive (value, index).
try.hint: Plain for loops. myReduce starts the accumulator at init.

checks.verify: assert(JSON.stringify(myMap([5, 6], (x, i) => x * i)) === "[0,6]", "map")
assert(JSON.stringify(myFilter([1, 2, 3, 4], (x) => x % 2 === 0)) === "[2,4]", "filter")

checks.t: myReduce folds with the initial value
checks.verify: assert(myReduce([1, 2, 3], (a, b) => a + b, 10) === 16 && myReduce([], (a, b) => a + b, 0) === 0, "reduce")

takeaway.key: map transforms, filter selects, reduce folds, find/some stop early. They return new values; sort (not toSorted) mutates.
mistakes: .map(parseInt).
reduce on a possibly empty array without an initial value.
Mutating the original array with sort/reverse/splice by accident.

problems.name: Apply Transform Over Each Element in Array

dryRun.title: curry((a, b, c) => a + b + c)
dryRun.note: Currying turns f(a, b, c) into a chain that collects arguments until it has fn.length of them, then calls f. Partial application fixes some arguments now and the rest later.

think.q:
const add = (a) => (b) => (c) => a + b + c
console.log(add(1)(2)(3), typeof add(1)(2))
why: Each call returns the next function until the last one adds.
think.exec:
const add = (a) => (b) => (c) => a + b + c
console.log(add(1)(2)(3), typeof add(1)(2))

think.q:
const f = (a, b = 2, c) => a
console.log(f.length)
why: length counts parameters before the first default. Generic curry helpers depend on length, so defaults break them.
think.exec:
const f = (a, b = 2, c) => a
console.log(f.length)

think.q:
const compose = (...fns) => (x) => fns.reduceRight((v, f) => f(v), x)
console.log(compose((x) => x + 1, (x) => x * 10)(2))
why: compose runs right to left: 2 × 10 = 20, then + 1 = 21.
think.exec:
const compose = (...fns) => (x) => fns.reduceRight((v, f) => f(v), x)
console.log(compose((x) => x + 1, (x) => x * 10)(2))

think.q:
const pipe = (...fns) => (x) => fns.reduce((v, f) => f(v), x)
console.log(pipe((x) => x + 1, (x) => x * 10)(2))
why: pipe runs left to right: 2 + 1 = 3, then × 10 = 30.
think.exec:
const pipe = (...fns) => (x) => fns.reduce((v, f) => f(v), x)
console.log(pipe((x) => x + 1, (x) => x * 10)(2))

think.q: Why curry a function like log(level)(message)?
opts: To make specialised versions once and reuse them, e.g. const warn = log("warn")
why: Currying is about reuse and composition, not speed.

try.task: Implement curry(fn): keep collecting arguments (one or many per call) until there are at least fn.length, then call fn.
try.hint: Return a function that takes ...args; if args.length >= fn.length call fn, else return a function that takes more and calls again with all of them.

checks.verify: const add3 = curry((a, b, c) => a + b + c); const one = add3(1); assert(one(2)(3) === 6 && one(10)(20) === 31, "reuse")

takeaway.key: Currying collects arguments until fn.length is reached. compose runs right-to-left, pipe left-to-right.
mistakes: Currying functions with default or rest parameters (fn.length is wrong).
Mixing up compose and pipe order.

dryRun.title: memoFib(5) with a cache
dryRun.note: Memoization stores results by input so repeated calls are instant. It only works for pure functions (same input → same output, no side effects), and the cache key must uniquely describe the input.

think.q:
let calls = 0
const sq = (x) => (calls++, x * x)
const cache = new Map()
const msq = (x) => cache.has(x) ? cache.get(x) : (cache.set(x, sq(x)), cache.get(x))
msq(3); msq(3); msq(4)
console.log(calls)
why: 3 is computed once, then read from the cache. 4 is new.

think.q:
const key = (...a) => a.join(',')
console.log(key(1, 23) === key(12, 3), key('1,2') === key(1, 2))
why: (1, 23) and (12, 3) give different strings, but "1,2" as a single argument collides with (1, 2). Use JSON.stringify(args) for safer keys.
think.exec:
const key = (...a) => a.join(',')
console.log(key(1, 23) === key(12, 3), key('1,2') === key(1, 2))

think.q:
const m = new Map()
m.set({ id: 1 }, 'x')

let n = 0
const now = () => ++n
const cache = {}
const memoNow = () => cache.v ?? (cache.v = now())
console.log(memoNow(), memoNow(), now())
why: Memoising an impure function freezes its first answer. That is a bug, not an optimisation.

think.q: What is the main cost of memoization?
opts: Memory: the cache grows with every new input unless you limit it
It makes the first call slower by 10x
why: Use a bounded cache (LRU) or WeakMap for object keys when inputs are many.

try.task: Implement memoize(fn) that caches by all arguments (use JSON.stringify(args) as the key) and exposes .calls() returning how many times fn really ran.
examples: const f = memoize((a, b) => a + b); f(1, 2); f(1, 2); f.calls()  // 1
try.hint: Keep a Map and a counter in the closure; attach a calls method to the returned function.

checks.verify: const f = memoize((a, b) => a + b); f(1, 2); f(1, 2); assert(f(1, 2) === 3 && f.calls() === 1, "cache")
const f = memoize((a, b) => a + b); f(1, 2); f(2, 1); assert(f.calls() === 2, "args")
let n = 0; const f = memoize(() => { n++; return 0 }); f(); f(); assert(n === 1, "0 must be cached")

takeaway.key: Cache results of pure functions by a key that fully describes the input. Watch memory and never memoise impure functions.
mistakes: Using cache[k] || compute() so 0/""/false results are never cached.
Weak keys like args.join(",").
Memoising functions that depend on time or outside state.
